title: The I/O Manager and the Driver Model
summary: Every read, write and device request in Windows becomes an **I/O request packet** (IRP) handed to a **stack** of drivers by the **I/O manager**. This lesson explains IRPs, driver and device objects, how a request travels down a device stack and its completion travels back up, the kinds of drivers (filter, function, bus), and the frameworks (WDM and KMDF) drivers are written with.
markdown:
## Requests as packets When a program calls `ReadFile` on a file or a device, the I/O manager in the kernel builds an **IRP**, a structure describing the request: | Part of an IRP | Meaning | |---|---| | **Major function** | What kind of request: `IRP_MJ_CREATE` (open), `IRP_MJ_READ`, `IRP_MJ_WRITE`, `IRP_MJ_DEVICE_CONTROL` (custom commands, lesson 16.05), `IRP_MJ_CLOSE` ... | | **Parameters** | Length, offset, the control code ... in the current **stack location** | | **Buffers** | Where the data is, described in one of three ways (lesson 16.07) | | **I/O status** | When finished: an NTSTATUS and how many bytes were transferred | The I/O manager then hands the IRP to the driver responsible for the target device. Drivers never call each other's functions directly; everything goes through IRPs. ## Driver objects and device objects | Object | One per | Holds | |---|---|---| | **Driver object** | Loaded driver | The table of **dispatch routines**: one function per major function the driver handles | | **Device object** | Device the driver manages (a disk, a port, or a purely software device like chapter 16's) | The device's state, and which driver handles it | When `DriverEntry` (lesson 16.02) runs, the driver fills its driver object's dispatch table: `driver->MajorFunction[IRP_MJ_READ] = EchoRead;`. When an IRP for one of its devices arrives, the I/O manager calls the matching routine. ## Device stacks Most hardware is handled by several drivers layered on top of each other, each adding something: ```mermaid flowchart TB U["ReadFile on the volume"] --> F1["Upper filter driver
e.g. encryption, antivirus scanning"] F1 --> FN["Function driver
e.g. the file system (NTFS) or the device's main driver"] FN --> F2["Lower filter driver"] F2 --> B["Bus driver
e.g. USB, PCI: talks to the bus the device is on"] B --> HW["Hardware"] B -.->|"completion travels back up"| F2 F2 -.-> FN FN -.-> F1 F1 -.-> U ``` Each driver, given an IRP, does one of three things: 1. **Complete it** itself (`IoCompleteRequest`) with a status, if it can satisfy the request. 2. **Pass it down** to the next driver in the stack (`IoCallDriver`), possibly after changing it, optionally asking to be told when it completes (a completion routine). 3. **Queue it** (mark it pending) to finish later, for example when hardware responds. The practice task simulates a request going down a stack until one driver completes it, and the completion coming back up through the drivers that asked to see it. | Kind of driver | Role | |---|---| | **Bus driver** | Discovers devices on a bus (PCI, USB) and creates their lowest device objects | | **Function driver** | The main driver for a device: knows how to operate it | | **Filter driver** | Sits above or below and adds or changes behaviour: encryption, compression, monitoring | | **Software-only driver** | No hardware; provides a service to user mode through a device object (chapter 16's driver is one) | ## Asynchronous by design Device I/O takes time. Rather than making the caller's thread wait inside the driver, an IRP can be **pending**: the driver returns `STATUS_PENDING` at once, and completes the IRP later from an interrupt or a worker. User mode sees this as overlapped (asynchronous) I/O, or simply as `ReadFile` returning when the I/O manager finally completes the request. This design is why Windows I/O can keep thousands of requests in flight. ## WDM and KMDF | Framework | Notes | |---|---| | **WDM** (Windows Driver Model) | The original model: drivers handle IRPs directly, including all the plug-and-play and power management requests. Powerful and error-prone | | **KMDF** (Kernel-Mode Driver Framework) | A library over WDM that handles the standard plug-and-play, power and queueing logic, and gives drivers objects with reference counting and cleanup. Microsoft's recommended choice for new drivers | | **UMDF** | Drivers for some device classes that run in **user mode**, so a bug crashes only a host process, not the machine. Preferred whenever the device type allows it | Chapter 16 starts with a minimal WDM-style driver to see the raw mechanism, and the same ideas carry over to KMDF. ## Common mistakes > [!warning] Completing an IRP and then touching it > After `IoCompleteRequest`, the IRP belongs to the I/O manager and may already be freed. > [!warning] Both completing and passing down the same IRP > Each IRP must be completed exactly once, by one driver. > [!warning] Writing a kernel driver when a user-mode one would do > UMDF, or an ordinary service, keeps bugs out of the kernel. ## Check yourself ```quiz ? What three things can a driver do with an IRP? - Read it, write it, or delete it - Copy it, encrypt it, or log it + Complete it, pass it down to the next driver in the stack, or mark it pending and complete it later - Send it to user mode, return it to the I/O manager, or ignore it > Ignoring an IRP leaves the caller waiting forever; every IRP must eventually be completed. ? What is the difference between a driver object and a device object? - They are the same object under two names + The driver object holds the dispatch routines; IRPs go to device objects - A driver object is in user mode; a device object is in kernel mode - A device object is the `.sys` file; a driver object is its process > One driver can manage many devices, each with its own device object. ? Name the kinds of drivers in a device stack. - Kernel drivers, user drivers and service drivers - Primary drivers, secondary drivers and backup drivers - Input drivers, output drivers and storage drivers + Bus drivers, function drivers and filter drivers > An IRP travels down the stack, and each driver can handle it or pass it on. ? What is an IRP? + A structure describing one I/O request - A kind of interrupt - A driver's configuration file > Major function, parameters, buffers and status. ? A filter driver receives an IRP it does not need to change. What does it do? - Completes it with success + Passes it down with `IoCallDriver` - Deletes it > Filters add behaviour only where they need to. ? Why is KMDF recommended over writing WDM drivers directly? - KMDF drivers run in user mode - WDM no longer works + It gets the standard driver logic right for you > UMDF is the user-mode framework. ```
ideas:
- Use Sysinternals WinObj to look at `\Driver` and `\Device`, and match a few devices to their drivers.
- Read the WDK documentation's "Example I/O Request - The Big Picture".
- Draw the device stack for a USB mouse, using Device Manager's **View → Devices by connection** to see the parent and child devices.

cards.q: What three things can a driver do with an IRP?
cards.a:
Complete it, pass it down to the next driver in the stack, or mark it pending and complete it later

Ignoring an IRP leaves the caller waiting forever; every IRP must eventually be completed.
